claims.text: CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloy can be fabricated by selective laser melting.
Standard SLM processing without preheating typically produces residual-stress-induced distortion and defect zones in CoCrFeNiMn.
Controlled build-chamber or substrate preheating during SLM reduces thermal gradients.
Reduced thermal gradients produce a more homogeneous microstructure.
Controlled preheating reduces fabrication-induced defects in SLM high-entropy alloys.
Preheating improves dimensional precision and mechanical integrity in SLM high-entropy-alloy components.
A preheating temperature of approximately 200–300 °C is sufficient to reduce thermal gradients without inducing oxidation.
Preheating reduces residual stresses during laser melting and solidification.
Preheating reduces porosity and microcracking.
Reducing the temperature differential between the melt pool and surrounding material moderates the cooling rate.
A moderated cooling rate minimizes thermal shock and residual stresses.
Lower residual stress decreases part warping and therefore improves dimensional accuracy.
Reducing defect-related weaknesses improves mechanical integrity.
Preheated components will adhere more closely to CAD specifications than room-temperature controls.
Preheated components will have higher strength and ductility than room-temperature controls.
SLM process-induced defects occur in as-built CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloy.
Non-preheated SLM parts have higher defect densities than preheated parts.
The benefit of preheating depends on avoiding oxidation, unwanted phase transformations, and high-temperature degradation.
The optimal preheating temperature and magnitude of improvement vary with alloy composition and SLM parameters.
Failure to obtain statistically significant improvements in dimensional accuracy, mechanical properties, and defect density relative to a non-preheated control would falsify the hypothesis.
